explain.say: Every minute your body needs a big supply of oxygen, and it all has to get from the air into your blood. The alveoli, tiny air sacs in your lungs, do this brilliantly. Let's find out what makes them so good at it.

faq.q: Why do alveoli need a large surface area?
faq.a: Diffusion can only happen across a surface. Hundreds of millions of alveoli give about 50 to 75 square metres, so lots of oxygen can enter the blood every second.
asks: Tell me about the huge surface area

faq.q: Why are alveolus walls so thin?
faq.a: The walls of the alveoli and capillaries are each one cell thick, so the gases only travel a very short distance, which makes diffusion fast.
asks: Tell me about the thin walls

faq.q: Why do alveoli need a good blood supply?
faq.a: Blood flowing through the capillaries carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide. This keeps a steep concentration gradient, so diffusion keeps going quickly.

faq.q: Why is the lining of the alveoli moist?
faq.a: Oxygen dissolves in the thin layer of moisture first, then diffuses across the walls into the blood.

faq.q: How does smoking affect the alveoli?
faq.a: Smoking can break down the walls between alveoli, a disease called emphysema. This reduces the surface area, so less oxygen reaches the blood and people get breathless.

facts: The total gas-exchange surface of adult human lungs is roughly 50 to 75 square metres.
The barrier between air and blood in the alveoli is less than one micrometre thick in many places.
